newsitem.title: USA: Allied Waste buys Laidlaw waste business for $1.5 billion.
newsitem.headline: Allied Waste buys Laidlaw waste business for $1.5 billion.

text.p: Allied Waste Industries Inc. said Wednesday it agreed to buy Laidlaw Inc.'s solid waste management business for $1.5 billion.

The acquisition will make Scottsdale, Ariz.-based Allied the nation's fourth-largest solid waste company, with annual 1996 revenues of $1 billion. Allied Waste reported 1995 revenues of $169.9 million.
It will do business in 23 states and seven Canadian provinces, with 49 landfills, 115 collection locations and 29 transfer stations.

Under terms of the deal, the Toronto-based Laidlaw will receive $1.2 billion cash, a 7 percent, 12-year subordinated debenture with a face amount of $150 million, and a 12-year zero-coupon subordinated note with a face amount of $168 million, Allied said.
Laidlaw will also receive 14.6 million shares of Allied Waste's common stock and 20.4 million warrants.
Following the news, Laidlaw Class B shares jumped C$1.05 (77 cents) to C$15.35 ($11.29) on the Toronto Stock Exchange, and Allied was up 25 cents at $9.375 on the Nasdaq market.
In a statement, Allied Waste said that on completion of the transaction, Laidlaw will hold 20 percent of its common shares.
The deal calls for Laidlaw to name two directors to Allied's board, expanding it to 12 members.
Allied said it expects the acquisition, which is expected to be completed by early 1997, will generate more than $60 million in cost savings.

"The acquisition of Laidlaw's North American solid waste management operations will, in one step, place Allied Waste among the industry's leading companies," said Roger Ramsey, chairman and chief executive officer of Allied Waste.

James Bullock, president and CEO of Laidlaw, said, "This transaction will allow our solid waste operations to become part of a highly skilled, rapidly growing company focused solely on solid waste management."
The transaction has already been approved by the boards of both companies. It is subject to a vote of Allied's stockholders and standard regulatory approvals.
Allied said it got commitments from Goldman, Sachs, Credit Suisse, and Citibank for a $1.2 billion bank credit facility to pay for the acquisition.
